Find when both runners are visible

question: Rachel and Robert run on a circular track. Rachel runs counterclockwise and completes a lap every \(90\) seconds, and Robert runs clockwise and completes a lap every \(80\) seconds. Both start from the start line at the same time. At some random time between \(10\) minutes and \(11\) minutes after they begin to run, a photographer standing inside the track takes a picture that shows one-fourth of the track, centered on the starting line. What is the probability that both Rachel and Robert are in the picture?
solution:
Use the standard interpretation that the photograph time is uniformly distributed between \(10\) and \(11\) minutes. In seconds, the sampling interval is \([600,660]\). Both runners must be visible at the same time, so we find the overlap of their visibility intervals.

The photographed quarter of the track extends one-eighth of a lap to each side of the starting line. A runner with lap time \(T\) is therefore visible from \(T/8\) seconds before each starting-line crossing until \(T/8\) seconds afterward. The opposite running directions do not change these intervals because the photographed arc is centered on the starting line.

Rachel crosses the starting line at multiples of \(90\) seconds. Only her crossing at \(630\) seconds has a visibility interval meeting \([600,660]\). Since \(90/8=11.25\), her interval is
\[
[618.75,641.25].
\]
Robert crosses at multiples of \(80\) seconds. Only his crossing at \(640\) seconds contributes. Since \(80/8=10\), his interval is
\[
[630,650].
\]
Their overlap is \([630,641.25]\), of length \(11.25\) seconds. Consequently,
\[
P=\frac{11.25}{660-600}=\boxed{\frac{3}{16}}.
\]
Including or excluding individual boundary times does not change this probability. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

edges.reason: The minute-second conversion explicitly uses the relation sixty seconds equals one minute established by the two time units.

Mental subtraction helps some minute differences. The endpoint only subtracts a single digit or whole tens mentally, whereas elapsed-time subtraction can use a written difference or count minute marks; a generic need for subtraction does not establish this specific procedure.

The explicit same-hour criterion is met by subtracting the minute readings. Hour/minute conversion prepares the broader cross-hour extension but is not required by that baseline; Gemini's hour-boundary argument adds that extension.

The earlier application endpoint explicitly distinguishes each-group amount from group count. Those meanings underlie the unit-price-times-quantity abstraction, as Gemini observes. Restrict this edge to that conceptual component rather than requiring two-digit arithmetic or a previously completed application lesson.
edges.scope: Per-unit amount and number-of-groups meanings in total-price and speed-times-time relationships

edges.reason: The normalized length, area or volume denotes an event likelihood in [0,1]. That numerical probability meaning is explicitly shared with cnm_285. Its finite equally-likely outcome-count algorithm is not required and is inapplicable to counting individual points in a continuum.
edges.scope: Only probability as a numerical likelihood in [0,1], common to every uniform measure model; finite equiprobable outcome counting is not required.
